data.title: The Road Less Congested: How Cities Are Rethinking Transport
data.passage:
A. For decades, city planners treated traffic as a problem to be solved by building more roads. The logic seemed simple: more lanes would mean less congestion, and faster journeys for everyone. However, the evidence from cities around the world tells a different story. Building new roads often attracts more cars, and the congestion returns within a few years. What matters is not the width of the road but how people choose to travel.

B. The foundation of any transport system is its infrastructure—the physical networks of roads, rails, and bridges. Many cities still rely on designs that were fixed decades ago, when car ownership was far lower. Yet the demands placed on these networks have changed dramatically. In practice, ageing infrastructure struggles to cope with modern volumes, and maintenance costs consume budgets that could be spent on alternatives.

C. One popular policy is to offer a subsidy to people who switch from driving to public transport. The idea is to reduce the number of cars on the road by making buses and trains cheaper. But subsidies alone rarely change behaviour for long. In fact, without reliable and frequent services, a fare reduction simply attracts people who were already using public transport, while drivers stay in their cars.

D. A resilient transport network is one that can absorb shocks—a sudden fuel shortage, a flood, or a pandemic—without collapsing. Such resilience comes from variety: multiple routes, different modes, and flexible capacity. However, resilience is often neglected in favour of efficiency. Yet the two are not opposites. A system with spare capacity may look wasteful on quiet days, but it keeps moving when conditions change.

E. The environmental case for changing how we travel is strong. Transport is a major source of carbon emission, and road vehicles account for a large share. But electric cars alone will not solve the problem. In practice, even zero-tailpipe vehicles produce emissions from tyre wear and electricity generation. What matters is reducing the total distance travelled by car, not just switching the fuel.

F. For many workers, the daily commute is the most fixed part of the day. It shapes where people live and how they spend their time. However, the pandemic proved that many journeys are not necessary. In fact, remote work has shown that a significant share of commuting can be avoided entirely, at least for office-based jobs. Yet for those who cannot work from home, the commute remains a daily burden.

G. Public transit is often presented as the obvious solution to urban mobility. Buses and trains move large numbers of people efficiently, using less space per passenger than cars. But transit systems face a funding paradox: they need high ridership to be efficient, yet low ridership makes them expensive to run. In practice, many systems struggle to attract riders because services are infrequent and unreliable.

H. The movement of goods—freight—is often overlooked in discussions of urban transport. Delivery vans and lorries are essential to the economy, bringing food and products to shops and homes. However, freight also contributes to congestion and pollution. Yet the solution is not to ban deliveries but to consolidate them: fewer, fuller vehicles can serve the same demand with less disruption.

I. Parking policy is a powerful but often ignored tool for managing demand. Minimum parking requirements, common in many cities, force developers to provide large car parks. However, these rules encourage driving by making it cheap and easy to park. In practice, removing such requirements can reduce car ownership and free up land for housing or green space.

J. The pedestrian is at the bottom of the transport hierarchy in most cities, yet walking is the most sustainable mode of all. However, pavements are often narrow, poorly lit, or missing entirely. In fact, cities that prioritise walking see fewer accidents and more vibrant street life. Yet investment in pedestrian infrastructure remains a small fraction of what is spent on roads.

K. Technology promises to make transport smarter. Real-time data can guide drivers away from congestion, and apps can help people plan multi-modal journeys. But technology is not a substitute for good policy. In practice, without pricing signals or restrictions, apps simply help more cars find the same crowded roads. What matters is using technology to support, not replace, structural change.

L. The most effective cities combine several approaches rather than relying on a single fix. They invest in transit, price parking, and redesign streets for pedestrians and cyclists. However, such changes are politically difficult because they disrupt existing habits. Yet the evidence from cities that have made the shift is clear: traffic falls, air quality improves, and streets become more liveable. In fact, the benefits extend beyond transport to public health and local economies.

M. Ultimately, the debate about urban transport is not about cars versus public transport. It is about how to allocate limited street space fairly and efficiently. However, that requires a shift in how success is measured—away from speed and towards access. Yet the most resilient systems are those that give people real choices, not those that simply move vehicles faster.
